questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Air Pollution and Its Causes' refers to.
questions.a: Air pollution is the undesirable change in the physical, chemical, or biological characteristics of air that adversely affects living organisms and the environment, caused by the introduction of particulate matter, toxic gases, and other harmful substances into the atmosphere.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Air Pollution and Its Causes'.
questions.a: Major air pollutants include particulate matter (PM), carbon monoxide (CO), nitrogen oxides (NOx), sulphur dioxide (SO2), hydrocarbons, and lead, which originate from combustion of fossil fuels, industrial processes, and vehicular emissions. These pollutants cause respiratory disorders, reduce visibility, and contribute to acid rain.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Air Pollution and Its Causes' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Air Pollution

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Water Pollution and Its Causes' refers to.
questions.a: Water pollution is the contamination of water bodies such as rivers, lakes, groundwater, and oceans by harmful substances including domestic sewage, industrial effluents, agricultural runoff, and heavy metals, which degrade water quality and harm aquatic life.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Water Pollution and Its Causes'.
questions.a: Key water pollutants include pathogens, organic matter (measured as BOD), plant nutrients (nitrogen and phosphorus), toxic heavy metals (mercury, cadmium, lead), and pesticides. Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD) is a measure of organic pollution; higher BOD indicates greater pollution. Mercury poisoning causes Minamata disease.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Water Pollution and Its Causes' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Water Pollution

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Soil Pollution' refers to.
questions.a: Soil pollution is the contamination of soil with harmful chemicals, heavy metals, pesticides, and solid waste that reduce soil fertility, alter its physical and chemical properties, and pose risks to human health and ecosystems.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Soil Pollution'.
questions.a: Soil pollutants include pesticides (insecticides, herbicides, fungicides), heavy metals (lead, mercury, arsenic), industrial wastes, and municipal solid waste. Pesticides like DDT persist in soil and enter food chains. Polyblend, a recycled plastic-based material, is used to improve soil durability. Bioremediation uses microorganisms to degrade pollutants.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Soil Pollution' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Soil Pollution

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Noise Pollution' refers to.
questions.a: Noise pollution is the unwanted, disturbing, or harmful sound in the environment that originates from human activities such as transportation, industrial operations, and construction, and which can cause hearing damage, psychological stress, and other health problems in humans and animals.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Noise Pollution'.
questions.a: Noise is measured in decibels (dB). Sounds above 80 dB are considered harmful. Major sources include vehicles, aircraft, industrial machinery, loudspeakers, and construction equipment. Effects include hearing loss, sleep disturbance, increased heart rate, hypertension, and reduced work efficiency. Control measures include sound-absorbing materials, planting trees, and restricting noise levels.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Noise Pollution' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Noise Pollution

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Deforestation and Its Consequences' refers to.
questions.a: Deforestation is the large-scale removal of forest cover, either by human activities such as logging, agriculture, and urbanisation, or by natural events, leading to loss of biodiversity, soil erosion, disruption of water cycles, and contribution to climate change.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Deforestation and Its Consequences'.
questions.a: Deforestation leads to loss of biodiversity, habitat destruction, soil erosion, increased CO2 in the atmosphere (contributing to global warming), disruption of the water cycle causing floods and droughts, and desertification. Reforestation and afforestation are key conservation strategies. The Forest Conservation Act (1980) and social forestry programmes aim to protect forest cover in India.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Deforestation and Its Consequences' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Deforestation

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Global Warming and Greenhouse Effect' refers to.
questions.a: Global warming is the gradual increase in the average temperature of the Earth's atmosphere and oceans, primarily due to the enhanced greenhouse effect caused by increased concentrations of greenhouse gases such as CO2, CH4, N2O, and CFCs resulting from human activities.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Global Warming and Greenhouse Effect'.
questions.a: Greenhouse gases (CO2, methane, nitrous oxide, CFCs, water vapour) trap infrared radiation re-radiated from the Earth's surface, warming the atmosphere. The greenhouse effect is natural and essential, but its enhancement due to anthropogenic emissions leads to global warming. Consequences include melting of polar ice caps, sea level rise, climate change, and changes in species distribution. The Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement aim to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Global Warming and Greenhouse Effect' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Global Warming

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Ozone Depletion' refers to.
questions.a: Ozone depletion refers to the thinning and breakdown of the stratospheric ozone layer, which protects life on Earth from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation, primarily caused by chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and other ozone-depleting substances released by human activities.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Ozone Depletion'.
questions.a: The ozone layer in the stratosphere absorbs harmful UV-B radiation (280-320 nm). CFCs released into the atmosphere break down in the stratosphere, releasing chlorine atoms that catalytically destroy ozone molecules. One chlorine atom can destroy up to 100,000 ozone molecules. The ozone hole was discovered over Antarctica in the 1980s. The Montreal Protocol (1987) aims to phase out CFC production. UV-B exposure causes skin cancer, cataracts, and reduced plant productivity.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Ozone Depletion' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Ozone Depletion

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Solid Waste Management' refers to.
questions.a: Solid waste management is the collection, treatment, and disposal of solid waste materials produced by human activities, including domestic, industrial, and agricultural waste, using methods such as landfilling, incineration, composting, and recycling to minimise environmental and health impacts.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Solid Waste Management'.
questions.a: Solid wastes include municipal waste (garbage), industrial waste, and biomedical waste. Improper disposal causes soil and water pollution and disease. Management strategies include reduce, reuse, recycle (3Rs), composting of biodegradable waste, sanitary landfills for non-biodegradable waste, and incineration for hazardous waste. Polyblend (recycled plastic waste mixed with bitumen) is used for road construction. E-waste is an emerging concern.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Solid Waste Management' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Solid Waste Management

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Conservation of Natural Resources' refers to.
questions.a: Conservation of natural resources is the sustainable management and protection of air, water, soil, forests, wildlife, and minerals through judicious use, legal protection, and restoration efforts to maintain ecological balance and ensure availability for future generations.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Conservation of Natural Resources'.
questions.a: Conservation strategies include afforestation, water conservation (rainwater harvesting, watershed management), wildlife protection through national parks and sanctuaries, sustainable agriculture, use of renewable energy, and implementation of environmental laws. Key legislation in India includes the Wildlife Protection Act (1972), Forest Conservation Act (1980), Water Act (1974), and Air Act (1981). Chipko Andolan and Silent Valley movement are notable conservation movements.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Conservation of Natural Resources' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Conservation
